decision_note: Aerides full text links the nectariferous spur to legitimate pollination and larceny/florivory with fruit-set consequences. Near-pass only because the focal floral state is generated by consumer damage or larceny rather than an independent do(A).
Aspidistra establishes obligate pollination plus larval pollen parasitism by the same midge system but does not test a declared floral attraction/display coordinate A against receiver responses.

Mount Cameroon full text records pollinators robbers and thieves across a floral-trait community gradient and finds a robber-versus-thief access-trait trade-off. Comparative receiver-overlap evidence only because no common reproductive outcome or do(A) is present.

Sanchez-Lafuente 2007 manipulates corolla lower-lip structure and measures pollinator response fruit-predator visitation and reproductive output. The antagonist response to A is null so this is a strict measurement-architecture pass rather than positive dual-audience conflict.

Brassica nigra herbivore treatments alter pollinator community composition florivore performance and seed set but the causal contrast is herbivore identity or induced state rather than a declared floral A coordinate.
Blueberry cultivar corolla morphology predicts legitimate visitor identity/visitation and nectar-robbing behaviour. No plant reproductive outcome or randomized A manipulation closes the strict chain.

Fitch and Vandermeer report that pollinators and nectar robbers prefer larger displays and robbery lowers reproduction. Survey and array estimates converge on an overrepresented flower-number optimum but the common reproductive outcome is not one randomized A surface.

Kula et al. report consistent Hadena preference for longer corolla tubes and associations of oviposition with both fruit initiation and later flower/fruit predation. The trait is observational rather than randomized.
The Silene-Hadena paper is a nine-population comparative genetic-structure analysis. It does not evaluate a declared floral A coordinate or its mutualist and antagonist response functions.

Rivest et al. evaluate pollen alkaloids against pollen thieves and legitimate pollinators. Thief abundance is unrelated to alkaloids and Bombus responses at natural thermopsine concentration are zero-compatible; no common plant reproductive outcome is linked to the same A contrast.
Wenninger et al. relate pollinators to flower density but seed predators to seed density. The two audiences therefore are not evaluated on the same declared floral coordinate A.

The Silene-Hadena-Microbotryum study measures oviposition against infection and floral traits but explicitly notes that visitation patterns to healthy versus infected flowers had not been specifically studied.

Symphytum shows nectar-robbing pressure triggering corolla abscission that enhances delayed self-pollination and seed set. The causal contrast is robber action causing a floral response rather than a predeclared A read by both audiences.

Irwin and Adler test floral morph and gelsemine expression with pollination and nectar-robbing responses across five populations. This is observational shared-trait evidence without randomized A or common reproductive fitness closure.
Lichtenberg et al. compare legitimate and nectar-robbing handling tactics and energetic efficiencies. The focal contrast is animal foraging tactic rather than a declared plant floral coordinate A.

Yoshikawa and Isagi separate bird-flower interactions into mutualistic and antagonistic subnetworks and show flower-size effects on feeding behaviour. No experimental A or common plant reproductive outcome is present.
